text: Chapter 10 Appendix: Rahab - A Woman of Faith

And God sent them there because He had a wonderful plan for Rahab's life. Rahab had already heard how God had delivered the Israelites from Egypt, parted the Red Sea, and given them many victories. Thus faith in Israel's God had already been born in her heart. She had begun to turn away from idols and had begun to place her trust in the true and living God. She told the spies as soon as they came, "I know that the LORD has given you the land… for the LORD your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath" (Joshua 2:9–11). This was a clear confession of her faith. And that was why God led the spies to her house.

Rahab's faith moved her to action—protecting the two Israelite spies, risking her life, and obeying the instructions given by the spies fully. Rahab acted on her faith and forsook everything she had in Jericho – thus proving that her faith was real. In this, she was so different from Lot's wife who looked back longingly at all her wealth that she had to give up in Sodom – and was immediately punished by God (Gen.19:23-26).
So Rahab was not only forgiven, but also woven into the royal lineage of Christ. God lifted her from shame and seated her among princes (Psalm 113:7 with Hebrews 11:31).
Chapter 10 Appendix: Rahab - A Woman of Faith
Faith That Acts Courageously

Rahab's sinful history did not disqualify her before God. God wiped her past clean. Her loyalty now was no longer to her Canaanite relatives and to Jericho - but to the God of Israel. She chose God's people over her culture, her city, and her past.
Rahab stands as a trophy of God's mercy. Her story assures us that no past is too dark and no life too broken, for God to redeem. He lifts us from the dust and puts us among His children.

Boaz 's father was Salmon – an Israelite from a well-respected family (Ruth 4:21). But Boaz's mother was Rahab – who was not only a Canaanite, but a prostitute in the Canaanite city of Jericho (Matthew 1:5).

When the king sent officers to her house to search for the Israeli spies, Rahab risked her life to protect the spies. She hid them under stalks of flax on her roof and misdirected the soldiers. Her faith was fearless when it came to doing what was right.

Interestingly, after her rescue, the Israelites kept Rahab and her family outside Israel's camp for a time – for some reason (Josh.6:23). Rahab could then have thought, "Here I have helped these people and now they are keeping me outside their camp like this". But she did not allow herself to think like that. Her humility was being tested – and she passed the test! She accepted the humiliation of being kept outside the camp.

Scripture records many godly women who stand as examples to us. But among those noble names, there is one that surprises us: Rahab the prostitute.

When the spies promised to save her life when Jericho would be captured, she asked them to spare the lives of her parents and her siblings as well. The spies agreed, on the condition that she would be faithful and hang the scarlet rope out of her window (through which they were going to climb down from her house - Josh.2:17,18). Rahab obeyed that instruction and gathered her family into her house and kept the plan secret.

Rahab's faith and humility were finally rewarded. She was welcomed into Israel – and later, even married Salmon, a leader from the tribe of Judah (Matthew 1:5). Their son was Boaz who became the husband of Ruth. And through that line came King David—and ultimately Jesus Himself
Share

Her name appears in Hebrews 11, the list of the "heroes of faith," alongside men and women whose lives were marked by remarkable faith in God. That God would choose Rahab — a woman who was well-known for her sinful past — as a heroine of faith is both astonishing as well as encouraging. It shows us that God picks up people from the worst of backgrounds and transforms them by His mercy. Rahab stands as a living illustration of this truth. God did not look at her past but forgave her and gave her a very blessed future.
